nameStory: White campion gets its name from its pure white flowers and its classification in the campion group, plants traditionally associated with open fields and meadows. The word 'campion' comes from the Old French 'champion,' referring to these hardy plants that thrive in disturbed, champion-like competitive growing conditions where other flowers might struggle.
description: White campion is a fuzzy, medium-height wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with distinctive white flowers that look like little stars. The entire plant feels soft and slightly sticky to the touch due to dense, fine hairs covering the stems and leaves. It starts as a low rosette of oval leaves, then sends up branching stems topped with clusters of white flowers that have deeply notched petals and balloon-like bases.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five white petals, each deeply notched like they were cut with scissors, creating a distinctive star-like appearance. The flower base is inflated like a small balloon and feels papery when gently squeezed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, feeling soft and slightly velvety due to dense fine hairs. Young plants form a basal rosette before sending up flowering stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Starts low and spreads outward, then develops forked, branching stems. The entire plant feels fuzzy and slightly sticky when touched, with a soft, almost flannel-like texture.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers open in evening and are most fragrant at night, growing in loose clusters at stem tips. Each flower is about 1 inch across with the distinctive inflated, balloon-like calyx behind the petals.

habitat: Look for white campion in disturbed soils like roadsides, field edges, waste places, and areas where the ground has been recently turned over. It thrives in full sun to partial shade and tolerates poor, dry soils where many other wildflowers can't compete.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as fuzzy rosettes of oval leaves close to the ground. Look for the characteristic soft, hairy texture even on small plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with white star-like flowers opening in evening and staying open through the morning. The balloon-like flower bases are most noticeable now.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into early autumn, with seed capsules developing inside the inflated flower bases. Plants become more branched and sprawling.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to germinate the following year. Occasionally short-lived perennials may persist as dried stems.

funFact: White campion flowers are 'night shift workers' - they open in the evening and release their strongest fragrance after dark to attract night-flying moths for pollination, then often close up during the hottest part of the day like botanical night owls!
confusionNotes: Often confused with bladder campion, but white campion is much fuzzier all over and has more deeply notched petals. Remember: white campion feels like soft flannel, while bladder campion feels smooth and waxy. Also, occasional pink-flowered plants are usually hybrids with red campion.
contextualKnowledge: Confusingly, white campion is sometimes called 'bladder campion' in the US, but true bladder campion (Silene vulgaris) is a different species entirely. This naming mix-up can make field guides tricky to navigate, so always check the scientific name when looking up campions.
compareHints: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother. Bladder campion has similar inflated flowers but smooth, waxy leaves instead of fuzzy ones. Red campion has similar fuzziness but pink flowers and grows in shadier, moister spots.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
